items.question: What is a hash table and how does it handle collisions?
items.answer: A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function.
items.reference: A hash table stores key-value pairs in buckets chosen by a hash function. Two different keys can land in the same bucket, which is a collision. Chaining keeps a list of entries per bucket, while open addressing probes for the next free slot.
good: What would happen in your table if two different keys hash to the same bucket?
How could one bucket keep two entries at once without losing either of them?
How would a lookup find the right entry when several keys share a bucket?

items.question: What is overfitting and how can you reduce it?
items.answer: Overfitting is when a model memorises the training data and does badly on new data.
items.reference: Regularisation adds a penalty on large weights so the model stays simple. Early stopping halts training when the validation error starts to rise. Cross-validation repeatedly holds out part of the data to estimate performance on unseen data. More training data also helps.
good: What could you add to the loss to discourage very large weights?
How would you notice during training that the model has started to memorise?
How would you estimate performance on data the model has never seen?

items.question: What is a database index?
items.reference: An index is a separate structure, often a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds up reads but adds cost to writes because the index must also be updated. A column with few distinct values gains little from an index.
good: What happens to the speed of inserts when a table has many indexes?
Why might an index on a column that holds only two different values help very little?
How does the database reach a row through the index without scanning every row?

items.question: What makes an API RESTful?
items.answer: It uses HTTP and URLs to identify resources.
items.reference: A RESTful API is stateless: each request carries everything the server needs, so the server keeps no session between requests. HTTP methods have meaning, and idempotent methods such as PUT can be retried safely without changing the result twice.
good: Why must every request carry all the information the server needs to answer it?
What would happen if a client retried a PUT request after a timeout?

items.question: How does gradient descent work?
items.answer: Gradient descent updates the parameters step by step to reduce the loss.
items.reference: Gradient descent moves the parameters against the gradient of the loss. The learning rate sets the step size: too large and the loss can overshoot or diverge, too small and training is slow. Stochastic variants use a small random batch of examples per step, which makes each step cheaper.
good: What could go wrong if each update step is far too large?
How would using a small random batch for each step change the cost of one update?

bad.q: How does gradient descent reduce the loss?

items.question: What is a race condition?
items.answer: It is a bug that happens when threads access shared data at the same time.
items.reference: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of threads touching shared data. A mutex or lock lets only one thread enter a critical section at a time. If two threads each wait for a lock the other holds, they deadlock.
good: How could you make sure only one thread updates a shared counter at a time?
What new problem could appear when two threads each wait for a lock the other one holds?
